speaker: N
text: In 1904, a horse in Berlin could do math better than most schoolchildren.

speaker: N
text: His name was Hans, and he answered by tapping his hoof.

speaker: N
text: Two plus three? Five taps.

speaker: N
text: The square root of sixteen? Four taps, and a proud little snort.

speaker: N
text: His owner, a retired math teacher, swore he had taught him everything himself.

speaker: N
text: Scientists rolled their eyes and came to expose the trick.

speaker: N
text: They searched for hidden signals, secret helpers, anything at all.

speaker: N
text: Nothing.

speaker: N
text: They sent the owner away and let strangers ask the questions.

speaker: N
text: Hans still got them right.

speaker: N
text: Meanwhile, a young student named Oskar noticed something strange.

speaker: N
text: When the person asking didn't know the answer, Hans got it wrong.

speaker: N
text: And when Hans wore blinders, his genius vanished completely.

speaker: N
text: You see, Hans couldn't count at all.

speaker: N
text: He was counting on us.

speaker: N
text: As his hoof got close to the right number, everyone watching tensed up without realizing it.

speaker: N
text: On the final tap, they relaxed, their heads lifted just a tiny bit, and Hans stopped.

speaker: N
text: Even Oskar, who knew the secret, couldn't stop himself from doing it.

speaker: N
text: Scientists still call it the Clever Hans effect, and it's why experiments today are run blind.

speaker: N
text: So Hans was a genius after all, just not at math.

speaker: N
text: He was a genius at reading people.

speaker: N
text: And we were so easy to read that the whole world believed...
